analysis.one_liner: Eliminates interest on federal student loans and refinances older loans at zero percent.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by Senator Welch in July 2023, referred to the Senate education committee, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make all existing federal student loans interest-free starting July 1, 2024, and refinance older, privately held federal loans into zero-interest direct loans. New loans would carry tiered rates from 0% to 4% depending on family income, with the highest rates still below what borrowers pay today. Loan repayments would go into a new Education Affordability Trust Fund, invested conservatively, with excess earnings able to fund extra Pell Grants.
analysis.who_benefits: About 43 million federal student loan borrowers, who would stop seeing balances grow from interest and pay off principal faster. Borrowers with older loans held by private companies would be refinanced into zero-interest loans without fees.

how_it_helps.text: Beginning July 1, 2024, no interest would accrue on existing Federal Direct Loans, applied automatically without borrower action, with an opt-out available [S2][S3].
Loans not held by the federal government, such as older FFEL and Perkins loans, would be refinanced into Federal Direct Consolidation Loans with no interest and no origination fees [S2][S3].

New loans made on or after July 1, 2024 would carry tiered rates based on the borrower's family income relative to local median income, capped at 4%, with 0% for borrowers at or below 400% of area median income [S2][S3].
Excess earnings from a new Education Affordability Trust Fund, funded by loan repayments, could be used for a Supplemental Pell Grant Program for low-income students [S2][S3].
Annual and aggregate student loan borrowing limits would be raised, with inflation adjustments, reflecting the higher cost of college [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government, which would forgo the interest income it currently collects on student loans. Higher-income borrowers would also lose the benefit of earning a return on keeping loans (forgone arbitrage), and the federal budget would show a larger cost. Taxpayers broadly would bear the cost of foregone interest revenue unless offset elsewhere.

drawbacks.text: The bill would forgo federal interest income on over a trillion dollars of student loans, a substantial cost to the federal budget that is not offset in the bill [S3].
The bill terminates interest-subsidized Stafford loans and replaces them with unsubsidized borrowing structures, a trade-off some would see as losing a targeted benefit even as rates fall [S3].

The new trust fund model shifts repayment flows into an investment vehicle whose board and managers would be making decisions about public funds with limited prior precedent, raising accountability questions [S3].

Higher-income borrowers could borrow at rates below the government's cost of funds, a benefit skewed toward those who least need it, since the income-based tiers only start at 400% of area median income [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the benefit is large and direct: balances stop growing and monthly payments go entirely to principal, shortening repayment. The main cost is fiscal: the federal government would collect far less interest revenue, and the bill does not identify an offset. Whether that is a fair trade depends on whether one views student loan interest as a profit center for the government or a program cost worth covering. The trust fund design is unusual and would carry governance and solvency questions Congress would need to work through.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in July 2023, and no further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Senator Welch introduced the bill on July 27, 2023 [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote occurred during the 118th Congress [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Borrowers gained nothing because the bill never advanced. The federal government continued collecting interest on student loans at prevailing rates, and the status quo of the student loan system remained intact.

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill after referral

against.name: Senate Majority Leader
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors, and never reached a vote, so no party split was recorded.

industries.note: The federal government currently earns interest on student loans; the bill would eliminate that revenue. Borrowers would save, but the federal budget would absorb the cost.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and refinancing companies
industries.note: Private companies that profit from interest and fees on student loans would lose customers to a zero-interest federal refinancing option.
The bill increases loan limits and could add supplemental Pell Grant funding, which schools would receive; the effect depends on how institutions use the additional capacity.
